title: Deterministic separability of nondeterministic timed languages
formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given two nondeterministic timed automata \(A,B\) with epsilon transitions over the same finite alphabet, always halts and decides whether there exists a deterministic timed automaton \(S\) such that \(L(A)\subseteq L(S)\) and \(L(S)\cap L(B)=\varnothing\)? Languages contain finite timed words. The separator may use any finite number of clocks and any finite integer constants: no resource bound is supplied or fixed in advance.
why: Deterministic timed descriptions support complement and monitoring operations that arbitrary nondeterministic descriptions do not. Settling unrestricted separability would identify whether the existence of such a classifier can be decided without an advance bound on the memory of time represented by clocks.
status_note: The primary 2020 paper and original problem page explicitly leave unrestricted deterministic separability open. A bounded search on 13 September 2026 did not identify a later resolution; no exhaustive current-status certification is claimed.

progress.text: The primary paper establishes the fixed-clock decidability results and explicitly leaves the unrestricted separator question open.

sentences: The input is a pair of nondeterministic timed automata describing finite event sequences with real timestamps.
The question is whether a terminating algorithm can decide the existence of a deterministic timed separator accepting the first language and rejecting the second.
Input automata may use invisible epsilon steps, while the separator has no such steps and may use any finite number of clocks.
The known decidability theorem fixes the separator’s clock count and therefore does not answer this unrestricted question.
Either a general decision procedure or an undecidability proof must be checked in Lean for the stated timed-word model.

definitions: A finite timed word over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) is \((a_1,t_1)\cdots(a_n,t_n)\), where \(n\geq0\), \(a_i\in\Sigma\), and \(0\leq t_1\leq\cdots\leq t_n\) are real timestamps. Equal timestamps and the empty word are allowed.

A timed automaton has finite sets of locations \(Q\), clocks \(X\), initial locations \(I\subseteq Q\), final locations \(F\subseteq Q\), and transitions \((p,a,\phi,Y,q)\). Here \(a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\), \(Y\subseteq X\), and \(\phi\) is a Boolean combination of true, false, \(x\mathrel{\sim} z\), and \(x-y\mathrel{\sim} z\), with clocks \(x,y\), integer \(z\), and \(\sim\in\{=,<,\leq,>,\geq\}\). There are no location invariants. All sets, transitions and guard formulas are explicitly encoded, with signed binary integer constants.

A run starts at time 0 in an initial location with all clocks zero. Time may advance by any nonnegative real amount, adding that amount to every clock. A transition can then fire when its guard is true; it changes the location and resets precisely the clocks in \(Y\) to zero. Its label and absolute firing time form an event. A finite run is accepting when its final location belongs to \(F\). The language \(L(A)\) consists of the timed words obtained from accepting runs by deleting all epsilon-labeled events and preserving the timestamps of all other events. Arbitrarily many but finitely many epsilon steps, including before the first and after the last visible event, are allowed.

A deterministic separator has exactly one initial location, no epsilon transitions, and at most one enabled transition for each location, input letter and clock valuation. Incomplete transition relations are permitted and a missing transition rejects. Equivalently one can merge overlapping guards when their target location and reset set coincide. The number of locations, number of clocks and magnitudes of constants can all depend on the input pair.

The decision algorithm is one ordinary deterministic Turing machine on the finite descriptions and must halt on every valid pair; no complexity bound or disjointness promise is imposed. A pair with intersecting languages necessarily has answer no. Malformed descriptions can be rejected.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of decidability for this input model and unrestricted finite separators, or a Lean-checked proof of its undecidability. Decidability for each fixed clock bound does not supply a decision algorithm for the unrestricted problem; the algorithm must also terminate on negative instances.

context_blocks.text: The problem asks whether two nondeterministically specified timed behaviors can be classified by a deterministic timed language. The accepted and rejected sets may leave other timed words unconstrained.

Theorem 1.1 of Clemente, Lasota and Piórkowski establishes decidability when the separator’s number of clocks is fixed, including when its largest constant is unrestricted. Their concluding section leaves unbounded-clock separability open. The paper’s undecidability theorem for unbounded timed synthesis is a separate game problem.

statement_review.notes: Recovered the primary finite-word model with epsilon input transitions, nondecreasing timestamps, diagonal integer guards and resets. Defined erasure including trailing epsilon events, epsilon-free deterministic separators and an unrestricted finite clock/constant budget. Distinguished the paper’s undecidable synthesis problem from open separability.
